questions.stem: The nurse on a cardiac step-down unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with heart failure whose weight is 0.5 kg higher than yesterday and who has trace ankle edema
A client 4 hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization with new low back pain; HR 118, BP 88/56
A client with atrial fibrillation taking warfarin whose INR this morning is 2.8 and who has no bleeding
A client with stable angina who asks for sublingual nitroglycerin before a planned walk in the hall

rationale.correct: After femoral catheterization, back or flank pain with tachycardia and hypotension is retroperitoneal bleeding until proven otherwise.

perOption.a: A small gain needs follow-up today, but it does not meet the 1 kg a day threshold and the client is stable.
perOption.b: Back pain with tachycardia and hypotension after femoral access suggests retroperitoneal bleeding and shock.
perOption.c: An INR of 2.8 is within the 2 to 3 target.
perOption.d: Taking nitroglycerin before exertion is an appropriate, planned use.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize a client with signs of retroperitoneal bleeding.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department reports crushing substernal chest pain. Blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg and heart rate 96/min. During the medication history the client says, "I took sildenafil last night." Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving it?

options.text: Aspirin 324 mg chewed now, before the ECG is read
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual every 5 minutes
12-lead ECG within 10 minutes
Troponin now and again in 3 hours

rationale.correct: Ask about phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) before any nitrate; together they can cause severe hypotension.

perOption.a: Aspirin is safe with sildenafil and is a core early treatment for acute coronary syndrome.
perOption.b: Nitrates within 24 to 48 hours of a PDE-5 inhibitor can cause profound hypotension.
perOption.c: An ECG is needed right away and has no interaction.
perOption.d: Serial troponins are standard and safe.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a nitrate contraindication.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the emergency department note for a client with chest pressure. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}} myocardial infarction, so the nurse should monitor closely for {{b2}}.

options.text: an anterior
an inferior
a lateral
bradycardia and heart block
a hypertensive crisis
hyperkalemia

rationale.correct: ST elevation in II, III and aVF shows an inferior MI, usually from right coronary artery occlusion; that artery commonly supplies the SA and AV nodes, so bradycardia and AV blocks are common.

perOption.b1:a: An anterior MI shows ST elevation in V1 to V4.
perOption.b1:b: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall.
perOption.b1:c: A lateral MI shows ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6.
perOption.b2:a: Right coronary artery occlusion often affects the SA and AV nodes, causing bradycardia and heart blocks.
perOption.b2:b: MI more often lowers blood pressure, especially an inferior MI with right ventricular involvement.
perOption.b2:c: Hyperkalemia is not a typical complication of the infarct location.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

exhibits.body:
Client, 61 years old, reports chest pressure and nausea for 40 minutes.

questions.stem: A client with a deep vein thrombosis is on a continuous IV heparin infusion. The 0600 aPTT is 122 seconds; the protocol's target is 60 to 85 seconds. The client has no bleeding, bruising or blood in the urine. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Continue the infusion and recheck the aPTT in 6 hours as planned
Stop or reduce the infusion as directed by the heparin protocol
Give vitamin K 10 mg subcutaneously to reverse the anticoagulant
Increase the rate by 2 units/kg/hr as the protocol allows for low levels

rationale.correct: A supratherapeutic aPTT on heparin is managed by the protocol: hold or reduce the infusion and recheck; protamine is for significant bleeding.

perOption.a: Continuing at this rate keeps the client at high risk of bleeding.
perOption.b: Heparin protocols direct holding or reducing the rate for a high aPTT, then rechecking.
perOption.c: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin.
perOption.d: Increasing the rate would raise the aPTT further.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a high aPTT on heparin.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with atrial fibrillation is going home on warfarin. Which statements by the client show correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I'll keep the amount of green leafy vegetables I eat about the same each week."
"I'll use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor."
"I'll call my provider if my stools turn black or tarry."
"I'll tell my dentist that I take warfarin."
"I can take aspirin or ibuprofen for a headache."
"If I miss a dose, I'll take two tablets the next day."

rationale.correct: Warfarin teaching: steady vitamin K intake, bleeding precautions, reporting signs of bleeding, telling all providers, and no doubling or NSAIDs.

perOption.a: Consistent vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable.
perOption.b: These reduce bleeding from minor injuries.
perOption.c: Black stools suggest GI bleeding.
perOption.d: Dental procedures may need planning.
perOption.e: Aspirin and NSAIDs increase bleeding risk; acetaminophen in moderation is preferred.
perOption.f: Doubling a dose raises the INR; the client follows the provider's missed-dose instructions.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate warfarin teaching.

questions.stem: A client taking digoxin 0.125 mg and furosemide 40 mg daily reports loss of appetite, nausea and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. Which laboratory result is most likely contributing to these findings?

options.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Calcium 9.2 mg/dL
Magnesium 2.0 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia all increase digoxin toxicity; loop diuretics commonly cause the low potassium.

perOption.a: Hypokalemia, often from loop diuretics, increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.
perOption.b: This sodium is normal.
perOption.c: This calcium is normal; high calcium would increase toxicity.
perOption.d: This magnesium is normal; low magnesium would increase toxicity.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Link electrolytes to digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: A client with a pulmonary embolism who weighs 80 kg has received an 80 units/kg heparin bolus and is now prescribed a heparin infusion at 18 units/kg/hr. The pharmacy supplies heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL of D5W. The baseline aPTT was 30 seconds. At what rate should the nurse set the infusion pump? Round to the nearest tenth.

rationale.correct: Dose: 18 units/kg/hr × 80 kg = 1,440 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. Rate: 1,440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 mL/hr. The bolus and aPTT are not used.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a weight-based heparin infusion rate.

questions.stem: The nurse finds an adult visitor collapsed and unresponsive in a hospital hallway. An AED is on the wall nearby. Place the nurse's actions in order, from first to last.

items.text: Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock
Make sure no one is touching the client and deliver the advised shock
Check responsiveness and shout for help and an AED
Attach the AED pads to the bare chest as soon as it arrives
Begin chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute
Check for breathing and a carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds

rationale.correct: Adult BLS: check, call, pulse and breathing check, compressions, AED as soon as available, shock, then resume compressions immediately.

perOption.a: Recognize the arrest and activate the response.
perOption.b: Confirm arrest quickly without delaying compressions.
perOption.c: Start high-quality CPR at once.
perOption.d: Early rhythm analysis guides defibrillation.
perOption.e: Clear everyone for safety, then shock.
perOption.f: Compressions restart without a pulse check.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Perform adult basic life support in order.

questions.stem: A client's monitor shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 180/min. The client has a palpable carotid pulse but is confused and pale, with a blood pressure of 72/40 mm Hg. The defibrillator is at the bedside. Which intervention should the nurse prepare for first?

options.text: Unsynchronized defibrillation
Synchronized cardioversion
Begin chest compressions
IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes

rationale.correct: Unstable VT with a pulse (hypotension, altered mental status) is treated with synchronized cardioversion; pulseless VT is defibrillated.

perOption.a: Unsynchronized shocks are for pulseless VT or VF.
perOption.b: VT with a pulse and signs of instability needs synchronized cardioversion.
perOption.c: The client has a pulse, so compressions are not indicated.
perOption.d: Amiodarone is for stable VT; this client is unstable.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client has had atrial fibrillation for an unknown length of time and has not been taking an anticoagulant. The client's heart rate is 96/min and blood pressure 128/76. The provider plans elective cardioversion today. Which test should the nurse expect before the cardioversion?

options.text: Transesophageal echocardiogram
Exercise stress test
Transthoracic echocardiogram only
48-hour Holter monitoring

rationale.correct: Atrial fibrillation of unknown or more than 48 hours' duration needs either 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a TEE to rule out clot before cardioversion.

perOption.a: A TEE checks the left atrial appendage for thrombus, which could embolize after cardioversion.
perOption.b: A stress test does not look for an atrial clot.
perOption.c: A surface echo cannot reliably see the left atrial appendage.
perOption.d: Holter monitoring records the rhythm but does not detect clots.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Anticipate testing before cardioversion.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing two clinic clients with leg symptoms, one with peripheral arterial disease and one with chronic venous insufficiency. For each finding, choose the condition it fits best.

rows.text: Calf pain while walking that goes away with rest
Brownish discoloration of the skin around the ankles
Thin, shiny, hairless skin on the lower legs
Shallow ulcer with irregular edges near the medial malleolus
Pain that eases when the legs hang over the side of the bed
Pitting edema of the lower legs by evening

rationale.correct: Arterial disease: claudication, thin hairless skin, deep ulcers, pain relieved by dependency. Venous disease: edema, brown staining, shallow medial ulcers, relief with elevation.

perOption.r1:c1: Intermittent claudication is classic for PAD.
perOption.r1:c2: Venous pain is aching and eases with elevation, not rest alone.
perOption.r2:c1: PAD causes pallor or dependent rubor.
perOption.r2:c2: Hemosiderin staining is typical of venous disease.
perOption.r3:c1: Poor arterial supply causes thin, hairless skin.
perOption.r3:c2: Venous disease causes thick, discolored skin.
perOption.r4:c1: Arterial ulcers are deep and punched out, often on the toes.
perOption.r4:c2: Venous ulcers are shallow and irregular near the medial ankle.
perOption.r5:c2: Venous symptoms worsen when the legs hang down.
perOption.r6:c1: Edema is not typical of PAD.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish arterial from venous disease.

questions.stem: A client 2 days after a total hip replacement suddenly says, "I can't catch my breath." Select the 4 findings that are most consistent with a pulmonary embolism.

options.text: Sharp chest pain that worsens on inspiration
Heart rate of 124/min
SpO2 of 86% on room air
"I feel like something terrible is about to happen"
Heart rate of 52/min
Thick yellow sputum and a productive cough for 3 days
Temperature of 38.9 °C (102 °F) with shaking chills

rationale.correct: PE: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia and anxiety, often after surgery or immobility.

perOption.a: Pleuritic chest pain is common with PE.
perOption.b: Tachycardia is the most common sign.
perOption.c: Hypoxemia results from the ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
perOption.d: A sense of impending doom is common.
perOption.g: High fever with chills suggests infection.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A client 2 days after a hip replacement suddenly becomes short of breath with pleuritic chest pain. The SpO2 is 86% on room air and the heart rate is 122/min. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Prepare the client for a CT pulmonary angiogram
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
Obtain a prescription for a heparin bolus
Draw a D-dimer level before calling the provider

rationale.correct: Suspected PE: support oxygenation first, call for help, then diagnostics and anticoagulation.

perOption.a: Imaging confirms PE, but oxygenation comes first.
perOption.b: Supporting oxygenation is the immediate priority.
perOption.c: Anticoagulation follows initial stabilization and assessment.
perOption.d: A D-dimer is less useful here and delays treatment.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Take first action for suspected PE.

questions.stem: A client started lisinopril 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago for hypertension. Which report from the client needs the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: "I've had a dry, tickly cough for about a week now."
"I feel a little dizzy when I stand up quickly in the morning."
"My lips and tongue started swelling up this morning."
"My lab report from yesterday says my potassium is 5.0."

rationale.correct: Angioedema from ACE inhibitors can happen at any time and threatens the airway; stop the drug and get emergency care.

perOption.a: A dry cough is common with ACE inhibitors and is reviewed, but it is not urgent.
perOption.b: Mild orthostatic dizziness needs teaching and follow-up.
perOption.c: Angioedema can obstruct the airway and needs emergency care.
perOption.d: A potassium of 5.0 is at the upper limit of normal.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize angioedema from an ACE inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old client newly diagnosed with primary hypertension (blood pressure 148/94 mm Hg on three visits) is starting lifestyle changes. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limit sodium to less than 2,300 mg a day
Aim for 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week
Eat more fruits, vegetables and low-fat dairy
Limit alcohol to 1 drink a day for women or 2 for men
Stop smoking
Stop the blood pressure medicine once readings are normal
Replace table salt with a salt substitute freely

rationale.correct: Lifestyle changes for hypertension: less sodium, DASH diet, activity, limited alcohol and no smoking, alongside prescribed medication.

perOption.a: Lower sodium lowers blood pressure; 1,500 mg is ideal for many.
perOption.b: Regular activity lowers blood pressure.
perOption.c: The DASH eating plan lowers blood pressure.
perOption.d: Heavy drinking raises blood pressure.
perOption.f: Normal readings usually mean the treatment is working.
perOption.g: Many substitutes contain potassium, which can be dangerous with some drugs; check first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach lifestyle changes for hypertension.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is due for furosemide 40 mg IV at 0900. This morning's potassium is 3.2 mEq/L and the client has had six premature ventricular contractions in the last hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the furosemide and recheck the potassium tomorrow morning
Give the furosemide with a glass of orange juice for potassium
Hold the furosemide and contact the provider about the potassium
Give the furosemide and ask the dietitian to add more potassium

rationale.correct: Check potassium before loop diuretics; hold and report hypokalemia, especially with dysrhythmias.

perOption.a: More diuresis would lower the potassium further while ectopy is present.
perOption.b: Diet cannot correct a low level quickly enough.
perOption.c: Hypokalemia with ventricular ectopy must be addressed before more potassium-wasting diuretic is given.
perOption.d: This delays correction of a low level with ectopy.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Hold a loop diuretic for hypokalemia.

questions.stem: One hour after a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery, the client says, "My groin feels warm and wet." The nurse finds bright red blood soaking the dressing. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Apply firm manual pressure just above the puncture site
Call the cardiologist to report the bleeding
Check the right pedal pulses and the color of the foot
Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees for comfort

rationale.correct: Active bleeding at a femoral puncture: apply firm pressure just above the site, then call for help and assess circulation.

perOption.a: Direct pressure over the arterial puncture controls the bleeding.
perOption.b: The provider is notified after the bleeding is controlled.
perOption.c: Distal checks matter, but stopping active bleeding comes first.
perOption.d: Hip flexion increases bleeding at the femoral site.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to femoral access-site bleeding.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with a known 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is awaiting elective repair next week and takes amlodipine for hypertension. Which finding needs the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: A pulsating mass felt in the periumbilical area
A bruit heard over the abdominal aorta
Sudden severe back pain and a BP of 86/50
A blood pressure of 138/86 mm Hg at rest

rationale.correct: Sudden severe back or abdominal pain with hypotension in a client with an AAA suggests rupture.

perOption.a: This is expected with a known aneurysm, and the area should not be palpated repeatedly.
perOption.b: A bruit is expected with turbulent flow.
perOption.c: These suggest rupture or expansion, a surgical emergency.
perOption.d: This needs control but is not an emergency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize aortic aneurysm rupture.

questions.stem: A client taking atorvastatin 40 mg daily calls the clinic. Which statement should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: "I take my pill in the evening with dinner."
"My muscles ache and my urine looks dark."
"I'm following a low-fat diet with more fish."
"I sometimes have mild constipation."

rationale.correct: Statins: report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine, which can mean rhabdomyolysis.

perOption.a: Timing is acceptable.
perOption.b: Muscle pain with dark urine suggests rhabdomyolysis.
perOption.c: This is appropriate.
perOption.d: This is a minor effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize statin-related muscle injury.

questions.stem: The charge nurse on a cardiac unit is making assignments. Which client is most appropriate to assign to a licensed practical nurse (LPN)?

options.text: A client just admitted with chest pain whose first troponin is pending
A client with stable heart failure who needs oral medications and a weight
A client who returned from a cardiac catheterization 30 minutes ago
A client who needs discharge teaching about a new direct oral anticoagulant

rationale.correct: Assign the LPN stable clients with predictable care; keep new, unstable or teaching-focused clients with the RN.

perOption.a: A new client with possible ACS needs RN assessment.
perOption.b: This stable client needs predictable care within LPN scope.
perOption.c: Early post-procedure care needs RN assessment because of bleeding risk.
perOption.d: Initial teaching is an RN responsibility.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign a cardiac client to an LPN.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes and a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization with contrast dye tomorrow. Which home medication should the nurse report to the provider before the procedure?

options.text: Metformin 1,000 mg twice a day
Atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime
Aspirin 81 mg daily
Omeprazole 20 mg each morning

rationale.correct: Contrast can impair kidney function, especially when it is already reduced; metformin is held per protocol and restarted once kidney function is confirmed.

perOption.a: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast because contrast kidney injury can cause metformin buildup and lactic acidosis.
perOption.b: Statins do not interact with contrast dye.
perOption.c: Aspirin is usually continued before catheterization.
perOption.d: Omeprazole does not affect contrast safety.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify medications to hold before a contrast procedure.

questions.stem: A client has returned to the unit after a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery. A closure device was not used. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the right leg straight for the prescribed time
Check the pulses, color and temperature of the right foot
Check the puncture site for bleeding or a hematoma
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees for meals
Help the client walk to the bathroom within the first hour

rationale.correct: After femoral access: keep the leg straight, check the site and distal circulation, encourage fluids and limit hip flexion.

perOption.a: Keeping the leg straight prevents bleeding at the arterial puncture.
perOption.b: Distal checks detect arterial occlusion or thrombus.
perOption.c: Bleeding is the most common complication.
perOption.d: Sharp hip flexion can cause bleeding; the head of the bed stays at 30 degrees or less at first.
perOption.e: Bed rest is needed for several hours after femoral access.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care after femoral cardiac catheterization.

questions.stem: A client with palpitations has a regular ventricular rate of 75/min on the monitor. The nurse sees sawtooth-shaped waves between the QRS complexes, four for each QRS. How should the nurse interpret this rhythm?

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter
Ventricular tachycardia
Sinus rhythm with PACs

rationale.correct: Atrial flutter: sawtooth flutter waves, often with a regular ventricular response at a fixed ratio.

perOption.a: Atrial fibrillation has a chaotic baseline and an irregularly irregular rhythm.
perOption.b: Sawtooth flutter waves with a fixed 4:1 conduction ratio are typical of atrial flutter.
perOption.c: VT has wide QRS complexes at a fast rate.
perOption.d: Sinus rhythm has one upright P wave before each QRS.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify atrial flutter on a rhythm strip.

questions.stem: A client's heart rate is 38/min in sinus bradycardia. The client is dizzy, pale and confused, with a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. IV access is in place. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first?

options.text: Atropine 1 mg IV push
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Metoprolol 5 mg IV over 2 minutes
Amiodarone 150 mg IV

rationale.correct: Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes up to 3 mg; if ineffective, transcutaneous pacing or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion.

perOption.a: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia.
perOption.b: Adenosine slows AV conduction and treats supraventricular tachycardia.
perOption.c: A beta-blocker would slow the heart rate further.
perOption.d: Amiodarone treats tachydysrhythmias.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat symptomatic bradycardia.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who had a permanent pacemaker placed in the left upper chest yesterday. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I won't lift my left arm above my shoulder for a few weeks."
"I'll carry my pacemaker ID card in my wallet."
"I'll keep my cell phone in my left shirt pocket so I hear it."
"I'll check my pulse and report it if it's below the set rate."

rationale.correct: Pacemaker teaching: limit arm movement on that side early, carry the ID card, keep magnets and phones away from the device, and check the pulse.

perOption.a: Limiting arm movement keeps the new leads in place.
perOption.b: The card informs providers and security staff.
perOption.c: Phones are kept about 15 cm (6 inches) from the device and held to the opposite ear.
perOption.d: A rate below the set rate may mean the pacemaker is not working properly.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate teaching after pacemaker insertion.
